toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

## plugin:desktop-commander:desktop-commander
Desktop Commander provides tools for working with the user's authorized device.
- Filesystem tools handle direct file and directory operations within configured access boundaries.
- Terminal process tools support shell commands, REPLs, and long-running processes. start_process creates a process session; interact_with_process sends input; read_process_output reads later output; force_terminate ends a session.
- Search tools are session-based. start_search creates a search session; get_more_search_results reads its results; stop_search ends it early.
- Absolute paths are generally the most reliable because relative paths depend on the active working directory.
- allowedDirectories and each tool's schema, annotations, and documented constraints define the operational boundaries.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination

## OCR (Tesseract Fallback)

Google Vision is not configured. Tesseract will be used for OCR but works poorly
on handwriting. For better results, either:
- Configure GOOGLE_VISION_API_KEY for Google Vision
- Set REMARKABLE_OCR_BACKEND=sampling to use this client's AI for OCR

## zotero-research
Read-only access to the user's Zotero research library. For substantive sport-science questions, build a Zotero-first evidence pack before answering. Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,
  task, card, or agent. Omit `BU_NAME` and reuse the default daemon for normal
  sequential local work across websites, tabs, screenshots, and Codex turns.
  Do not invent per-job names such as `gmail1375` or `slack1371`: every new
  local daemon opens another browser-level CDP connection and Chrome may show
  another Allow prompt.
- Set `BH_TAB_MARKER=0` before starting the daemon to leave page titles unchanged.
  The horse marker remains enabled by default.
- A timeout or page that pauses while hidden is not permission to foreground
  Chrome. Keep using background CDP operations. For a focus-gated page,
  temporarily call `cdp("Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled", enabled=True)`,
  perform and verify the operation, then disable it in a `finally` block. If
  background control still cannot work, report that limitation instead of
  activating the tab. Do not invent a `Runtime.evaluate` scroll replacement or
  a cross-frame JS walker.
- The normal local flow attaches to the running Chrome/Chromium CDP endpoint. No browser ids or local profile selection.

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name

- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them

- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

Take the first option that fully works:

---
name: skill-bloat-and-promotion
description: "Measured skill bloat in this setup, the project-until-promoted rule that fixes it, and the command that re-measures usage from .jsonl session logs"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: f1097c6d-9db5-4bb5-a0f7-c42d645cf75d
  modified: 2026-10-07T16:20:14.842Z
---

Measured 2026-09-12 from a gap analysis of a Nate Herk / **Mark Kashef** video
("How to Actually Choose the Right AI Agent", 2026-09-11). Full note:
`~/SecondBrain/Inbox/2026-09-12-harness-over-model-mark-kashef.md`.
Same shape as the earlier audit in [[brain-audit-loop]] — that one scored the
**vault**, this one scores the **skill layer**.

## The measurement

| Metric | Count |
|---|---|
| Global skills in `~/.claude/skills/` | 160 (→ **117** after the Tier 1 archive, 2026-09-12) |
| Plugin skills exposed per session | ~37 (6 enabled, 18 disabled) |
| SKILL.md files in plugin cache | 606 — disabled plugins + old versions, NOT the load |
| Project-level skills anywhere in `~/DEV` | **0** |
| `.jsonl` sessions scanned | 414 |
| Distinct real skills **ever** invoked | **58** |
| Used 3+ times | 30 |
| Used exactly once | 19 |

Everything is global. That is the anti-pattern, not the achievement.

## The rule that fixes it — promotion

**Everything stays project-level until it earns global.** A skill lives in
`<project>/.claude/skills/` until it proves itself across 2+ projects, then it
gets promoted to `~/.claude/skills/`. Keeps the global load small and the blast
radius tight — so when something underperforms you can tell a *model* problem
from a *harness* problem from an *organisation* problem.

## The audit question

Not "how often did I run this skill?" but **"would the model do this fine without
the skill now?"** A skill is a crutch; as the brain gets smarter the crutch starts
to *limit* it. Seasonal skills (`forecast-capture`) and occasional ones
(`ingest-book`) are low-count by design — low usage alone is not a delete signal.

## Re-measure (BUILTIN filter is the whole trick)

Without the `BUILTIN` set you also count `/exit`, `/clear`, `/compact` and friends,
which inflates the total to 74 and buries the real skills.

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF'
import glob,re,collections
BUILTIN={'exit','clear','compact','rename','color','login','logout','plugin','doctor',
'help','model','config','resume','cost','status','init','agents','mcp','hooks','memory',
'review','vim','terminal-setup','install-github-app','add-dir','bug','release-notes',
'pr-comments','ide','permissions','statusline','output-style','todos','export',
'privacy-settings','upgrade','fast','artifacts','tasks','loop','context','usage','rewind',
'sandbox','feedback','worktrees','skills','reload-skills','reload-plugins','bashes',
'keybindings','theme'}
c=collections.Counter()
for f in glob.glob('/Users/kristinarash/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl',recursive=True):
    try:
        for line in open(f,encoding='utf-8',errors='ignore'):
            if 'Skill' not in line and 'command-name' not in line: continue
            for m in re.finditer(r'"name"\s*:\s*"Skill"\s*,\s*"input"\s*:\s*\{[^}]*?"skill"\s*:\s*"([^"]+)"', line):
                c[m.group(1)]+=1
            for m in re.finditer(r'<command-name>/([a-zA-Z0-9:_-]+)</command-name>', line):
                c[m.group(1)]+=1
    except Exception: pass
real={k:v for k,v in c.items() if k.split(':')[-1] not in BUILTIN and k not in BUILTIN}
print("distinct real skills ever invoked:",len(real))
print("used >=3 times:",len([k for k,v in real.items() if v>=3]))
print("used exactly once:",len([k for k,v in real.items() if v==1]))
for k,v in sorted(real.items(),key=lambda x:-x[1]): print(f"{v:5d}  {k}")
EOF
```

## Decision, 2026-09-12

**Do the skill audit BEFORE adopting Pi** (`pi.dev`) as an alternative harness.
Rationale: the leverage is the bloat, not the harness. Auditing first means any

Installing a third-party (vendored, upstream-owned) skill on this setup: **clone the repo
into `~/.agents/skills/<name>` — the one real directory — then symlink it into the four
harness folders.** Established by the six that predate it (`humanizer`, `pp-espn`,
`articulation-skill`, `game-film-timestamps`, `pp-fireflies`, `session-handoff`).

```
~/.agents/skills/<name>        ← the clone; Codex/Cursor/Copilot read here natively
~/.claude/skills/<name>   →    symlink    Claude Code
~/.gemini/skills/<name>   →    symlink    Gemini CLI
~/.codex/skills/<name>    →    symlink    Codex
~/.cursor/skills/<name>   →    symlink    Cursor
```

One clone means one `git pull` updates every harness. Claude Code registers a new skill
**live, mid-session** — no restart needed.

**Windows trap — `ln -s` silently copies.** Git Bash's default `ln -s` duplicates the
directory instead of linking. Claude Code still finds the skill, so it *looks* installed,
but the copy has no `.git` and `git pull` silently stops being the update path. Use
`MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict ln -s <target> <link>`, and verify from PowerShell —
`(Get-Item <path> -Force).LinkType` must print `SymbolicLink`. `ls -la` in Git Bash shows
`l... ->` for both cases, so it is **not** sufficient proof on its own. Same MSYS family as
[[git-bash-msys-ad-stall]], different mechanism.

**The nightly-backup jam.** `~/.claude/skills` is its own repo with a `pre-commit` hook
that refuses any symlink (git mode 120000), while `daily-backup.ps1` runs `git add -A` on
it. So a freshly added third-party symlink sits as `?? <name>` and will **jam the nightly
backup commit** until the exclude block is regenerated.

**The fix is `~/.claude/skills/sync-to-codex.ps1`, not a hand edit.** It classifies every
symlink in `~/.claude/skills` as THIRD_PARTY, drops it from the git index ("removed
third-party link '<name>' from the index (left on disk)"), and rewrites the generated block
in `.git/info/exclude` — which is marked *"Rewritten on every sync. Per-machine. Do not
edit by hand."* Supports `DRY_RUN=1`; dry-run first and confirm zero `retire`/`REFUSE`/
`FATAL` lines before applying.

**Why the sync cannot clobber the clone:** its copy loop touches only `$MANAGED` entries
(real directories in canonical with a SKILL.md), and its retirement loop only removes names
present in the *previous* manifest. A third-party name enters neither list, so
`~/.agents/skills/<name>` and its `.git` survive every sync. Verified — sync ran clean over
41 managed + 7 third-party with the clone intact on `main`.

**Do not route these through `CreateSkill`.** Canonicalizing an upstream repo (TitleCase,
`Workflows/`) rewrites files git tracks and breaks `git pull`. The `skills/CLAUDE.md`
mandate governs skills Eric *owns*, not vendored ones.

**Nothing propagates to the Mac.** `skills/` is gitignored out of the dotclaude repo and
`~/.agents` is not a repo at all, so each machine needs its own clone + symlinks.

Installing a third-party (vendored, upstream-owned) skill on this setup: **clone the repo
into `~/.agents/skills/<name>` — the one real directory — then symlink it into the four
harness folders.** Established by the six that predate it (`humanizer`, `pp-espn`,
`articulation-skill`, `game-film-timestamps`, `pp-fireflies`, `session-handoff`).

```
~/.agents/skills/<name>        ← the clone; Codex/Cursor/Copilot read here natively
~/.claude/skills/<name>   →    symlink    Claude Code
~/.gemini/skills/<name>   →    symlink    Gemini CLI
~/.codex/skills/<name>    →    symlink    Codex
~/.cursor/skills/<name>   →    symlink    Cursor
```

One clone means one `git pull` updates every harness. Claude Code registers a new skill
**live, mid-session** — no restart needed.

**Windows trap — `ln -s` silently copies.** Git Bash's default `ln -s` duplicates the
directory instead of linking. Claude Code still finds the skill, so it *looks* installed,
but the copy has no `.git` and `git pull` silently stops being the update path. Use
`MSYS=winsymlinks:nativestrict ln -s <target> <link>`, and verify from PowerShell —
`(Get-Item <path> -Force).LinkType` must print `SymbolicLink`. `ls -la` in Git Bash shows
`l... ->` for both cases, so it is **not** sufficient proof on its own. Same MSYS family as
[[git-bash-msys-ad-stall]], different mechanism.

**The nightly-backup jam.** `~/.claude/skills` is its own repo with a `pre-commit` hook
that refuses any symlink (git mode 120000), while `daily-backup.ps1` runs `git add -A` on
it. So a freshly added third-party symlink sits as `?? <name>` and will **jam the nightly
backup commit** until the exclude block is regenerated.

**The fix is `~/.claude/skills/sync-to-codex.ps1`, not a hand edit.** It classifies every
symlink in `~/.claude/skills` as THIRD_PARTY, drops it from the git index ("removed
third-party link '<name>' from the index (left on disk)"), and rewrites the generated block
in `.git/info/exclude` — which is marked *"Rewritten on every sync. Per-machine. Do not
edit by hand."* Supports `DRY_RUN=1`; dry-run first and confirm zero `retire`/`REFUSE`/
`FATAL` lines before applying.

**Why the sync cannot clobber the clone:** its copy loop touches only `$MANAGED` entries
(real directories in canonical with a SKILL.md), and its retirement loop only removes names
present in the *previous* manifest. A third-party name enters neither list, so
`~/.agents/skills/<name>` and its `.git` survive every sync. Verified — sync ran clean over
41 managed + 7 third-party with the clone intact on `main`.

**Do not route these through `CreateSkill`.** Canonicalizing an upstream repo (TitleCase,
`Workflows/`) rewrites files git tracks and breaks `git pull`. The `skills/CLAUDE.md`
mandate governs skills Eric *owns*, not vendored ones.

**Nothing propagates to the Mac.** `skills/` is gitignored out of the dotclaude repo and
`~/.agents` is not a repo at all, so each machine needs its own clone + symlinks.

Established 2026-09-18 installing `grill-with-ui`. Related:
[[dev-layout-and-discovery]], [[keystoneos-verification-habits]]

**My recommendation is not to install the plugin. Copy its rules instead.** The useful part is one short prompt. The rest of the package adds more automation to a setup you have already been trimming.

**What it is.** Ponytail tells the agent to write the smallest change that fully works. Before writing new code it climbs a ladder:
1. Does this need to exist at all?
2. Is it already in this codebase?
3. Does the standard library do it?
4. Does a package you already have do it?
5. Can it be one line?
6. Only then, write the minimum.

It never cuts validation, error handling or security. It leaves one small test for any risky logic, and every reply ends with what was skipped and any risk. The whole idea is in `skills/ponytail/SKILL.md`, which is about 3.5 KB.

**What installing the plugin would add:**
- **Three hooks:**
  - The rules plus a 2,000-character map of the codebase get injected at every session start.
  - The rules get injected again into every subagent.
  - A hook runs on every prompt you send.
- **The "band":** a cost and token tracker. By default it writes a CSV per project and an HTML board to `~/.config/ponytail/band/`. Its import command reads all your past Claude Code session logs. Nothing leaves the machine unless you set a webhook, which is off by default. I checked the code to confirm that.
- **Five extra commands:** review, audit, debt, gain and help.

**Why it doesn't fit your setup:**
- **It breaks your own rule.** Your harness-time-budget rule says a new tool must replace an old one. Ponytail replaces nothing.
  - `/ponytail-review` overlaps `mattpocock-skills:code-review` and `codex-review`.
  - `/ponytail-audit` overlaps graphify and `/improve-codebase-architecture`.
  - The band overlaps `explain-usage` and `agent-cost-report`.
- **Your session start is already crowded:** the Keystone snapshot, superpowers, context-mode and the memory injection all load there. Adding the ponytail rules and a codebase map on top of that, on every session, is the kind of always-on weight you cut 66% of in the 9/12 skill audit.
- **The benchmarks are the author's own,** run on FastAPI + React web apps. Your work is mostly Python and R data pipelines, and its codebase map doesn't read R at all.
- **It changes how every reply ends,** which could clash with your output-style rules.

**What it gets right:** "reuse what exists before writing new code" and "end with what you skipped and the risk" are good habits. They match how you already like to work (small steps, don't break mid-season work). Six to eight lines in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` would capture most of the value with no hooks to maintain.

If you'd rather test the real thing, the cheap trial is to enable it in one repo only at `lite` level with the band ledger off, then compare a week of diffs.

Separately, the session-start hook reported failures you should know about:
- **daily-backup:** 7 errors since 10-15, including repo pushes and session-snapshot archives. See `~/.claude/scripts/logs/daily-backup.log`.
- **Memory compiler:** flush failures, a stale lock and a backlog.
- **claude-files-digest:** one failed send, for 10-17.
- **gps-pull:** the 10-17 coach report is missing `coach_report.pdf`.

The backup and GPS ones look worth a look first.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\plugins\cache\mattpocock\mattpocock-skills\1.3.1\skills\productivity\writing-for-agents

Reference for writing any document an agent consumes: a skill, an `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`, a doc reached by a pointer. The packaging differs; the writing does not: the same levers make each one predictable, since the agent takes the same _process_ every run rather than producing the same output.

When the document you're writing is a skill, read [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md) for frontmatter, invocation choice, and router skills.

## Context pointers

A **context pointer** is a reference held in the agent's context that names some out-of-context material and encodes the condition for reaching it. A skill's description is one; a line in `AGENTS.md` naming a doc is the same object. The pointer's _wording_, not its target, decides when the agent reaches the material, and how reliably. A must-have target behind a weakly worded pointer is a variance bug: sharpen the wording first, and inline the material only if sharpening fails.

A pointer does two jobs: state what the material is, and list the **branches** that should trigger reaching it (a branch is a distinct case the document handles, so different runs take different paths through it). Every word of an always-loaded pointer costs on every turn, so it earns even harder pruning than the body:

- **Front-load the leading word**: the pointer is where it does its triggering work.
- **One trigger per branch.** Synonyms that rename a single branch are one branch written twice; collapse them and keep only genuinely distinct branches.
- **Cut identity the body already carries.**

## The two loads

Every document and pointer you add spends one of two budgets:

- **Context load** is the cost of always-loaded material on the agent's window: an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill description, anything sitting in context every turn, spending tokens and attention whether or not it fires.
- **Cognitive load** is the cost on the human: which documents exist and when to reach for each. The human is the index. Not a cost to minimise: it is the price of human agency; spend it where human judgement matters, remove it where it does not.

Material reached only through a pointer escapes context load at the price of the pointer's own line; material with no pointer at all rides entirely on cognitive load.

## Information hierarchy

A document is built from two content types: **steps** (the ordered actions the agent performs) and **reference** (definitions, rules, facts consulted on demand). The two mix freely: all steps (a recipe), all reference (a review's rules, this skill), or both. The core decision is where each piece sits on the **information hierarchy**, a ladder ranked by how immediately the agent needs the material:

1. **In-file step** is the primary tier: what the agent does, in order.
2. **In-file reference** is consulted on demand. Often a legitimately flat peer-set (every rule of a review on one rung), which is a fine arrangement, not a smell.
3. **Disclosed reference** is pushed out into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, loaded only when the pointer fires. Spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference that lives anywhere and any document can point at.

Push too little down and the top bloats; push too much and you hide material the agent actually needs. That tension is the whole decision.

**Progressive disclosure** is the move down the ladder (out of the main file and behind a pointer) so the top stays legible. Not primarily a token optimisation: it is how the hierarchy is protected. Branching is the cleanest disclosure test: inline what every branch needs, and push behind a pointer what only some branches reach. When a document has steps, in-file reference that should be disclosed buries them and turns attending to them into a coin-flip: a variance lever, not just a legibility one.

**Co-location** is the within-file companion: where the ladder decides _how far down_ a piece sits, co-location decides _what sits beside it_ once there. Keep a concept's definition, rules, and caveats under one heading rather than scattered, so reading one part brings its neighbours with it. The test: the document should read like documentation written for the agent. Grouped material reads that way; scattered material does not. (Distinct from duplication: that repeats one meaning in two places; scattering fragments one meaning across many.)

**Sprawl** is the failure mode here: a document simply too long, even when every line is live and unique. Attention thins across the excess, and every extra line is one more to keep relevant. The cure is the ladder: disclose reference behind pointers, and split by branch or sequence so each path carries only what it needs.

## Steps and completion criteria

Every step ends on a **completion criterion**, the condition that tells the agent the work is done. Two properties make it a lever:

- **Clarity**: can the agent tell done from not-done? A vague bound ("understanding reached") invites **premature completion**: ending the step before it is genuinely done, attention slipping to _being done_. The visible steps still ahead (the **post-completion steps**) supply the pull; the criterion's clarity is the resistance. Defend in order: **sharpen the bound first** (local and cheap); only if it is irreducibly fuzzy _and_ you observe the rush, hide the later steps by splitting the sequence. Hiding only works across a real context boundary (a hand-off or a subagent dispatch; an inline call leaves the later steps in context and clears nothing).
- **Demand**: how much it requires. "Every modified model accounted for" forces thorough work where "produce a change list" does not. Demand drives **legwork** (the digging the agent does within the work, latent in the wording rather than written as its own step), and it is not step-bound: "every rule applied" binds a body of flat reference just as "every step done" binds a sequence, which is how an all-reference document still carries an exhaustiveness bar.

The strongest criteria are both checkable and exhaustive.

## When to split

Splitting one document into two spends one of the two loads, so split only when the cut earns it:

The packaging differs; the writing does not: the same levers make each one predictable, since the agent takes the same _process_ every run rather than producing the same output.

## Context pointers

A **context pointer** is a reference held in the agent's context that names some out-of-context material and encodes the condition for reaching it. A skill's description is one; a line in `AGENTS.md` naming a doc is the same object. The pointer's _wording_, not its target, decides when the agent reaches the material, and how reliably. A must-have target behind a weakly worded pointer is a variance bug: sharpen the wording first, and inline the material only if sharpening fails.

A pointer does two jobs: state what the material is, and list the **branches** that should trigger reaching it (a branch is a distinct case the document handles, so different runs take different paths through it). Every word of an always-loaded pointer costs on every turn, so it earns even harder pruning than the body:

- **Front-load the leading word**: the pointer is where it does its triggering work.
- **One trigger per branch.** Synonyms that rename a single branch are one branch written twice; collapse them and keep only genuinely distinct branches.
- **Cut identity the body already carries.**

## The two loads

Every document and pointer you add spends one of two budgets:

- **Context load** is the cost of always-loaded material on the agent's window: an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill description, anything sitting in context every turn, spending tokens and attention whether or not it fires.
- **Cognitive load** is the cost on the human: which documents exist and when to reach for each. The human is the index. Not a cost to minimise: it is the price of human agency; spend it where human judgement matters, remove it where it does not.

Material reached only through a pointer escapes context load at the price of the pointer's own line; material with no pointer at all rides entirely on cognitive load.

## Information hierarchy

A document is built from two content types: **steps** (the ordered actions the agent performs) and **reference** (definitions, rules, facts consulted on demand). The two mix freely: all steps (a recipe), all reference (a review's rules, this skill), or both. The core decision is where each piece sits on the **information hierarchy**, a ladder ranked by how immediately the agent needs the material:

1. **In-file step** is the primary tier: what the agent does, in order.
2. **In-file reference** is consulted on demand. Often a legitimately flat peer-set (every rule of a review on one rung), which is a fine arrangement, not a smell.
3. **Disclosed reference** is pushed out into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, loaded only when the pointer fires. Spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference that lives anywhere and any document can point at.

Push too little down and the top bloats; push too much and you hide material the agent actually needs. That tension is the whole decision.

**Progressive disclosure** is the move down the ladder (out of the main file and behind a pointer) so the top stays legible. Not primarily a token optimisation: it is how the hierarchy is protected. Branching is the cleanest disclosure test: inline what every branch needs, and push behind a pointer what only some branches reach. When a document has steps, in-file reference that should be disclosed buries them and turns attending to them into a coin-flip: a variance lever, not just a legibility one.

**Co-location** is the within-file companion: where the ladder decides _how far down_ a piece sits, co-location decides _what sits beside it_ once there. Keep a concept's definition, rules, and caveats under one heading rather than scattered, so reading one part brings its neighbours with it. # Machine

Machine-specific shell, paths, and traps live in `~/.claude/machine.md` (gitignored; copy `machine.macos.md` or `machine.windows.md` to `machine.md` on a new machine). It is imported below.

@machine.md

Two machines share this setup: the MacBook (`~/DEV`) and the Baylor Windows laptop (`~/Desktop/DEV`). Projects sync through GitHub (`erash11`), documents through Google Drive.

**Session routine.** When working inside a project repo, follow the Session routine in its `AGENTS.md`: `git pull` and read `docs/STATUS.md` at the start; update `STATUS.md`, commit, and `git push` at the end. This is what keeps the two machines in step.

# Workflow Expectations

- When asked to **create, merge, or consolidate an artifact** (calendar, deck, doc), finish with the produced file in hand. Check what exists first, then build the file even when a similar one already exists.
- **Saving, moving, or backing up a file** → read `~/.claude/STORAGE.md` first. It says where each kind of file lives.
- When the user types `/graphify`, invoke the Skill tool with `skill: "graphify"` before doing anything else.
- Skills are tools: invoke one when it clearly fits the task.

# Session Startup

The `keystone-unified-snapshot.js` SessionStart hook injects `global-memory/USER.md`, `global-memory/MEMORY.md`, a summary of `transcripts/.errors.log` (only when non-empty), and a pointer to the KeystoneOS snapshot. Work from the injected copy.

- If hook failures appear, surface them once on the first response, then continue. Entries mean a hook or scheduled job failed.
- If a **"SessionStart hook could not read a required memory file"** block appears, say so on the first response.
- **If no `## User profile` block is in context at session start, the hook did not fire.** Say so, then read `USER.md`, `MEMORY.md` and `transcripts/.errors.log` by hand.
- The injection is a frozen snapshot: mid-session writes take effect next session. Load anything further only when a question needs it.

# Memory — routing only

The two-tier memory system (`~/.claude/global-memory/` and `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`) is owned by the **`memory-write` skill**, which holds the tier rules, character caps, slug rules, write steps, retrieval ladder, and daily-compiled-log rules.

The active project's Tier A memory (`~/.claude/projects/<slug>/memory/`, indexed by its `MEMORY.md`) is **auto-injected by the harness** each session. Tier A files are also indexed by memsearch, so they stay recallable across projects.

- Writing a fact — "remember this", "note that", "save this", "forget about" → `Skill("memory-write")`
- Recalling past context — "did we already…?", "what did we decide about X" → `Skill("memory-write")`, retrieval-ladder section
- Daily compiled logs at `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/daily/` are written only by `claude-memory-compiler`. Read one only when a question needs that day.
- **Slugs differ per machine** (Mac `-Users-kristinarash-DEV-<X>`, Windows `C--Users-eric-rash-Desktop-DEV-<X>`). Tier A written on one is not auto-injected on the other; memsearch still finds it. Durable project facts belong in the repo's `docs/` so both machines see them.

---

Maintainer note: `AGENTS.md` diverges from this file on purpose (Codex has no Skill tool, so it spells out the memory rules). Keep them as separate files; the memory procedure's one home is the `memory-write` skill.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

This one file serves Claude Code, Codex and Cowork (uploaded to claude.ai). Cowork has no TaskList and no Claude Code memory hooks: do what applies there and say what was skipped.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- **Registry drift.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py crosswalk` (`portfolio_json` is in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json`). It compares `portfolio.json` with every DEV folder and Drive `01_PROJECTS` folder and only reports; it never moves anything. Do not fix drift during closeout. List each item it found under "Still open", naming any folder created this session first: that is a project started without a row, the exact way projects got lost before the 2026-10-03 organization pass. `drive_unreachable` means the Drive checks never ran; say so, do not call it clean. Cowork cannot run it; say it was skipped.
- **7-day rule.** Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py seven-day --apply`. Name any project it paused, and any project on its last two days, under "Still open" with what it still needs (a receiver, step 1). Revive with the board's status pill or `portfolio.py` once there is a first step to show.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- **Registry edits get their own commit.** In project-triage, if `git status --porcelain portfolio.json` shows a change (board edits from the day, `set-status`, `set-receiver`), commit that file alone first as `data: board edits <YYYY-MM-DD>`, then the rest. The board header's "N unpushed registry edits" counts these; a skipped one becomes a JSON merge conflict when the other machine edits too.
- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- If `~/.claude/mods` changed this session (a mod added, edited or `.disabled`), run the mods sync (`bash ~/.claude/mods/mods-sync.sh` on the Mac, `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\mods\mods-sync.ps1` on Windows) and list any invalid mod under "Still open".
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- **Deliverables.** A finished file made for someone else this session (PDF, deck, report, sheet) gets a copy at `~/DEV/_DRIVE/03_REPORTS/YYYY-MM-DD_<Sport>_<Topic>_<Audience>.<ext>`. The repo keeps the source; Drive keeps the handed-off copy. Name the copy in the report.
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours. On a Cowork-only day it may be absent; say so, it is not an error.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first. Item 1 is one concrete action (a command to run or a file to open), not a theme: it is the line `~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py` shows Eric the next morning
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric, each one written out in full as its own top-level bullet: the question itself and enough context to answer it without opening another file. Never a pointer ("See PLAN.md"): `/startup` reads this section across every repo with `where-was-i.py --decisions`, and a pointer gives no question to answer. Mark answered items `ANSWERED <date>: …` or strike them through (`~~…~~`) so they drop off that list. Leave the section empty, not "-", when nothing is waiting.
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

Then run `python ~/.claude/scripts/where-was-i.py --decisions --days 1`. It prints exactly what tomorrow's `/startup` will show as "Decisions waiting on you". Every decision this session left open must appear there as a readable question; if one is missing or shows as a pointer, fix that repo's `## Open questions` before the commit.

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

**Keep the resume cards true (PM system design Decision 9).** The live board shows each project as a card read from STATUS and the registry; if a card doesn't make sense tonight, it won't in six weeks. Run `python <dir of portfolio_json>/landed.py scan --days 1` (about a minute), then `python <dir of portfolio_json>/portfolio.py card-check`. It prints the card of every registry project touched today, on either machine, with its gaps. Fix each gap before the Step 2 commit:

- `STATUS has no entry dated <today>`: add `- <today>: <what happened>` under the repo's Done / Current state.
- `STATUS has no Next item`: put one concrete action first under `## Next`.
- `no next step (next_action)` (Drive-only row): set it on the board or with `portfolio.py add-update <name> "<note>" --next-action "<step>"`.
- `needs a receiver`: `portfolio.py set-receiver <name> "<who>"` (a name, or `me: <why>`). Ask Eric when it is not obvious from the session; never invent one.
- `touched but marked <status>`: revive it (`portfolio.py set-status <name> active`) or say in STATUS why a retired project was touched.

Re-run `card-check` after the fixes. Its output is the last section of the report (**Cards:**); trim to projects with work today if it is long, but never drop one that still has a gap.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what> / skipped (Cowork, no hooks)
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Registry drift:** <N items, or "none"> (`portfolio.py crosswalk`)
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.

**Cards:** <`portfolio.py card-check` output, after the Step 4 fixes>
```

The cards come last on purpose: they are what the next session, on either machine, picks up from.

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

**Where everything landed.** Build that list from the ledger, not from memory: the Step 4 `landed.py scan --days 1` already refreshed it (it reads git in every DEV repo and file times on Drive and the vault, so files written by scripts and shell copies are included); run `landed.py show --days 1`. Put its project-grouped output in the report under **Landed:** (trim to the projects this session touched if it is long). # RTP_Constraints_Course

A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).

**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
phase of return to performance in American football.

## How to work here

Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.

Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |
| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |
| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. 0001 written 2026-09-03 (opposed vs unopposed). |
| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. `course-map.html` is the 8-lesson plan Joe sees. |
| `reference/gray-infographics/` | Local copies of Rob Gray's free infographics, saved 2026-09-03 because the site is one person's. Includes the 21-study comparative table, extracted and searchable. **Do not republish, do not commit.** See its `README.md`. |
| `sources/` | Full-text books and long PDFs obtained legitimately. Author-supplied — **never redistribute, never commit.** Holds the Myszka book (240 pages, printed 14–253), its OCR text sidecar, the reversible scan manifest, and the extracted bibliography. |
| `scripts/` | `export_for_joe.py` builds the offline package Joe gets on Drive (strips private links; leak check must pass). `velocity_band_sheet.py` builds the Baylor velocity-band sheet (Harries' levels from GPS; writes to Drive only, since it names athletes). Also the book-scan pipeline. `scan_pipeline.py` turns phone photos into a page-ordered OCR'd PDF and **refuses to rename unless the arithmetic gate passes**; `verify_pdf.py` proves page order afterwards by an independent route. Read `scan_pipeline.py`'s docstring before the next scanning job — it carries every trap found so far. |
| `docs/handoffs/` | Durable cross-session handoffs. Newest first. |
| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. 0001 records the lesson-0001 hook decision and Joe's starting floor. |

## Rules specific to this workspace

- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.
- **Every lesson ends in something Joe could do at practice tomorrow.**
- `GLOSSARY.md` does not exist yet by design — see `NOTES.md`.
- **Phase 2 is a drill-design tool.** Do not start it until the lessons have specified it.
  Route: `/grill-with-docs` → `/prototype` → `/implement`. Local-only per Baylor IT.

## Source library

Papers referenced as `LIB/…` live in `~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/research-papers/`.
Search with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`. Zotero MCP was down on 2026-09-01.
